newsitem.title: USA: U.S. plane again attacks Iraqi mobile missile site.
newsitem.headline: U.S. plane again attacks Iraqi mobile missile site.

text.p: A U.S. F-16 fighter jet fired a missile at an Iraqi mobile anti-aircraft missile site on Monday, the second incident in three days, the Pentagon said.

A Defence Department spokesman said that, as in Saturday's incident, the pilot's instruments indicated his aircraft was being targeted from the ground as he patrolled the no-fly zone in southern Iraq.
After investigating the earlier incident, however, the Pentagon said the Iraqi radar had not actually targeted the American jet.

The spokesman, Navy Cmdr. Joe March, said Monday's missile firing took place at about noon Iraq time (0900 GMT) about 25 miles (40 km) from where Saturday's incident occurred. The United States has warned Iraq not to threaten U.S. and other allied pilots patrolling the zone, established after the Gulf War to restrict Iraqi military activity.
"An F-16 pilot assigned to the 4404th fighter wing fired a HARM (missile) after receiving an indication that his aircraft was being targeted by an Iraqi mobile surface-to-air system," March said.

As on Saturday, the F-16 returned to its base in the Gulf region safely. March said there was no indication of damage to the missile site from the High-speed Anti-radiation Missile designed to seek out radar signals and destroy such sites.

White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry, travelling with President Bill Clinton on a campaign trip in Manchester, New Hampshire, said: "The president will be briefed on the situation ... and we're looking into it further.

"We don't see any pattern here that the situation has changed," McCurry said, referring to Iraqi President Saddam Hussein's previously announced decision to comply with the no-fly zone and not fire at allied planes patrolling it.

The Defence Department issued a statement late on Sunday saying that "further analysis of Saturday's incident involving a U.S. aircraft over southern Iraq has not substantiated initial indications of Iraqi radar activity."

A Pentagon spokesman said an investigation was continuing into the incident and it was unclear whether the radar activity picked up by instruments aboard the Air Force F-16 was due to an equipment malfunction.

But he defended the pilot's actions and said he "acted appropriately" in accordance with the rules of engagement for Western forces patrolling the no-fly zone. Those rules permit pilots to attack any radar site that is illuminating their aircraft in a threatening way.

Iraq denied Saturday's incident occurred at all. The Iraqi News Agency quoted a Foreign Ministry spokesman dismissing the White House statement as "false news" aimed at helping Clinton win re-election and saying Iraq was still committed to a decision not to fire at U.S. and allied jets patrolling the two no-fly zones in southern and northern Iraq.

The decision was taken in September after a confrontation with the United States because of Baghdad's military backing for a Kurdish group against a rival in the north. The United States responded by attacking southern Iraq with missiles and extending the southern no-fly zone for Iraqi planes to the outskirts of Baghdad.
